hyperbole

/hy-PER-buh-lee/ - four syllables ending in 'lee,' with the stress on PER · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration so extreme that no one is meant to take it literally.

Sports radio runs on hyperbole: every August, at least one caller declares the rookie 'the greatest athlete the species has produced.'

Example

Uncle Ray's fishing stories run on hyperbole — a bass 'the size of a canoe,' mosquitoes 'big enough to saddle,' a winter 'so cold the words froze in the air' — and nobody at the table reaches for a tape measure.

Hyperbole is the exact word because the stretching is deliberate and meant to be seen through: the fun depends on everyone knowing the bass was not boat-sized. A claim that quietly hopes to be believed has crossed into different territory; hyperbole performs its exaggeration in the open.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overstatement: An overstatement pushes a claim past the facts while still asking to be believed — the home ground of overstated, taught in this same unit. Hyperbole blows the claim up so far that belief is never the point; the listener is meant to see through it.

hype: Hype is promotional inflation — relentless talking-up designed to sell tickets, products, or candidates, and it wants to be believed. Hyperbole is a figure of speech: one spectacular impossibility, offered as flavor rather than fact.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

understatement: putting a thing more mildly than the truth, and trusting the gap to speak

literal truth: saying exactly what is, with no stretch in either direction

Where it sits · how far past literal truth the stretch goes

stretch → hyperbole → tall tale

stretch vs. hyperbole: A stretch is far milder than hyperbole: calling a good chili 'the best in the county' pushes the truth a notch and still hopes to be believed, while hyperbole vaults past belief on purpose — 'this chili could power the grid.'

tall tale vs. hyperbole: A tall tale goes beyond hyperbole: hyperbole is one impossible flourish inside ordinary talk, while a tall tale chains flourish to flourish into a whole story and dares the listener to object.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — hyper-: over, beyond (Greek)

Root — bole: a throwing (Greek ballein, to throw)

Put it together: Hyper- (over, beyond) + bole (a throwing) = 'a throwing beyond.' Greek ballein, to throw, seeded a whole family of throw-words in English, and hyperbole is the claim thrown clean over the truth — launched past the literal on purpose.

Use the root in a new word: emblem: The maple leaf works as an emblem far beyond Canada's borders, stitched onto backpacks by travelers who never need to explain it.

Root Check

Word Choice

playful / rhetorical

Hyperbole names the figure of speech, not the lie: speaker and listener share the joke, so the word carries analysis rather than accusation. If the claim expects belief, call it overstated — that word is taught in this same unit and keeps the dispute about degree. And when the exaggeration is a portrait of a person rather than a claim, you are looking at caricature, also in this unit.
